passage:
Hi Sonali,

Before Saturday, can we try something? Imagine it's Sunday evening and we lost. Why? I wrote down two big reasons. One: the venue's internet is patchy, and our model needs a download. Two: I'm the only one who has written any code so far, so if I get stuck or fall ill, we're finished. Here's what I've done about them. I booked a phone data plan for the weekend and already saved the model files on the laptop. And I split the app into three parts: mine is the model, yours is the front end, and Ravi has the data cleaning. Can you look at the split and tell me if the front end is too much?

Tejas

qa.a: Tejas is worried about being the only coder, since getting stuck or ill would leave the team unable to finish.

qa.q: What other step could the team add to lower the risk further?
qa.a: The team could hold a short check-in each evening to see who is stuck, since a problem found early is easier to share out.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel about the front-end part?
qa.a: Sonali may feel a little pressed by the workload but relieved that the coding is now shared.

grounding: Shows a student team imagining losing a hackathon, listing weak internet and one person doing all the coding, then booking a data plan and splitting the work among three.

passage:
You want the real story of how we placed second at the city hackathon, Vishal? I'm Saurabh, I was there, so here it is.
Two weeks before, the three of us sat in the library and I said, let's pretend we've already lost. What went wrong? Rhea said straight away, "The college Wi-Fi died during the demo." Then Imran said, a bit quietly, "I did all the code at 3 a.m. and nobody else understood it." Which was exactly what happened last year.
So we took each one and made it a task. Wi-Fi: I booked a separate hotspot and a backup phone plan. One-person coding: we split the app into three modules, login, map and alerts, one each, with a check-in every evening.
On the day, the Wi-Fi did drop for twenty minutes. We just switched to the hotspot and kept going.

qa.q: How was the app split among the three team members?
qa.a: It was split into three modules, login, map and alerts, one each.

qa.q: What might Imran have been feeling when speaking up about last year?
qa.a: Imran was probably a bit embarrassed and tired of carrying everything, which is why the words came out quietly.

qa.q: What else could the team turn into a preventive step before the next hackathon?
qa.a: They could plan a short practice demo a day early, so any gaps in the presentation show up before the judges see it.

qa.q: How might the judges have seen the team when the Wi-Fi dropped?
qa.a: The judges probably saw a calm team that switched to the hotspot and kept going, which makes the team look prepared rather than lucky.

grounding: It shows a student team imagining losing a hackathon, naming weak internet and one person doing all the code, then booking a hotspot and splitting modules among three.

I'm Jyoti, I sit next to Tejas's team in the lab, and the week before the hackathon they were strange to watch.
On Monday they stood at the whiteboard and Tejas wrote in big letters: WE LOST. WHY? I thought it was a joke. Then they started filling it. "Network dies." "Laptop crashes." "Only Tejas knows the backend."
By Wednesday each line had a name and a fix next to it. Someone had a pocket hotspot on the desk. The backend was split into three parts with three different people's names on sticky notes, and Tejas was teaching the other two how the database worked.
On the day of the hackathon, their laptop froze during setup, and they carried on from a second one with the same code. I don't know if Tejas was calm inside. He looked calm.

qa.q: What did Tejas write on the whiteboard on Monday?
qa.a: Tejas wrote WE LOST. WHY? in big letters.

qa.q: What does Tejas looking calm on the hackathon day suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Tejas felt prepared and fairly confident, though Jyoti admits not knowing what was going on inside.

qa.q: What else could Tejas's team add to their list, and why?
qa.a: They could add a timed rehearsal of the pitch, since running out of time while presenting is another common way hackathon teams lose.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see the team's week of planning?
qa.a: Jyoti first thinks the whiteboard is a joke, then watches the fixes appear and sees the team handle the frozen laptop smoothly.

grounding: It shows a student team imagining failure, listing weak network and one person holding the backend, then getting a hotspot and splitting the work among three.
